patch.objective: Explain that types are erased before code runs, so run-time input still needs checking
secondaryObjectives: Choose unknown over any for untrusted values, and narrow before using them

sources.cite: TypeScript Handbook, TypeScript for the New Programmer
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: the compiler 'erases the types to produce the resulting compiled code'; 'the type system itself has no bearing on how your program works when it runs'; TypeScript 'never changes the runtime behavior of JavaScript code'. The case: a shipping field typed as a number arrives as a string at run time and is concatenated; only a check at the boundary (Number() with a NaN test) catches it.

sources.cite: Addition (+), MDN Web Docs JavaScript reference (last modified 2026-05-11)
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch 2026-11-16. Relevant text: 'If one side is a string, the other operand is also converted to a string and they are concatenated'; example '"2" + 2; // "22"'. What parseFloat, parseInt, Number() and unary plus return for the strings in the case ('99.985.00' parses to 99.985 with parseFloat and to NaN with Number or unary plus; parseInt('5.99') is 5) is standard JavaScript behavior not on the fetched page.
